title.narrative: ILO 2020-2024 Social dialogue and workers' rights

description.narrative:
Insatsen är en förlängning och vidareutveckling av befintligt ILO-samarbete i Etiopien (2015-2018). Målet är att främja produktiva arbetstillfällen med rimliga arbetsvillkor i Etiopien, i synnerhet för fattiga kvinnor och ungdomar.
Produktiv sysselsättning är den viktigaste länken mellan ekonomisk tillväxt och fattigdomsminskning. Projektets syfte är att bidra till nationell utveckling genom att stödja framväxten av en hållbar textil och beklädnadsindustri. Projektet fokuserar på stärkt social dialog, förbättrade relationer bland arbetsmarknadens parter, ökad produktivitet, etablering av minimilöner och förbättrade arbetsvillkor.
ILO kommer stödja arbetsmarknadens parter och staten i implementeringen av den nyligen godkända arbetslagstiftningen och etableringen av ett system för minimilöner för anständiga levnadsvillkor. På företagsnivå kommer projektet bidra till förbättrade mekanismer för konfliktlösning och arbetsplatsinformation och dialog för ökad produktivitet, förbättrade arbetsförhållanden, minskad personalomsättning och reduktion av resursbortfall.
Programmet förväntas leda till: 1. Förbättrat arbetarnas välbefinnande när det gäller inkomst, säkerhet, jämlikhet, rättigheter, röst och representation, 2. Högre industriproduktivitet och konkurrenskraft, och 3. Förbättrad ansvarsskyldighet och öppenhet i arbetsförvaltningen.
Vidare bidrar det föreslagna projektet till kanaler för att stärka den demokratiska utvecklingen och rättighetsagendan.

The intervention is an extension and expansion of current collaboration with ILO in Ethiopia (2015-2018). The objective is to contribute to the creation of productive employment with decent working conditions in Ethiopia, in particular for poor women and youth.
Productive employment is the strongest link between economic growth and poverty alleviation. The aim of the project is to contribute to national development by supporting sustainable textile and garment industry. The focus will be on improved social dialogue, improved collaboration among labour market actors, improved productivity, establishment of miminum wages, and improved working conditions.
The ILO will support the Ethiopian social partners and government in implementing the recently approved labour legislation and establishing a system for minimum wages that can provide for decent living standards for the workers. At the enterprise level, the project will facilitate the establishment of grievance handling, workplace information-sharing and labour-management consultation mechanisms aiming to promote inclusive as well as enhanced productivity through lean production, improved working conditions, reduced turnover of staff and minimising waste of production.
The intervention is expected to lead to: - Improved worker wellbeing in terms of income, safety, equality, rights, voice and representation, - Higher industry productivity and competitiveness, and - Enhanced accountability and transparency in labour administration.
In addition, the suggested programme contributes to channels for strenthened democracy and Human Rights.

The overall objective of the programme is to contribute to poverty reduction by improved working conditions and incomes for people working in the textile sector. The program aims to promote rights at work, encourage decent employment generation, and strengthen tripartite social dialogue between governments, trade unions and employers’ organizations in Ethiopia. The program focuses on both the policy and regulatory challenges to reforming the business enabling environment and its value for increasing exports and international investment as well as the importance of advancing continuous improvement of wages and working conditions through improved industrial relations, and the role of women’s empowerment within Ethiopia. For example, the ILO will support the Ethiopian social partners and government in implementing the recently approved labour legislation and establishing a system for minimum wages that can provide for decent living standards for the workers. At the enterprise level, the project will facilitate the establishment of workplace information-sharing and labour-management consultation mechanisms aiming to promote enhanced productivity through lean production, improved working conditions, reduced turnover of staff and minimising waste of production. As such, the program seeks to support fair, transparent, efficient and effective procedures for the prevention and resolution of workplace conflicts and grievances through social dialouge and collective bargaining. The intervention is expected to result in: - Improved workers wellbeing in terms of income, safety, equality, rights, voice and representation, - Higher industry productivity and competitiveness, and - Enhanced accountability and transparency in labour administration. Programmatic set-up The overall programme composes of and seeks to combine and coordinate several different ILO projects for improved effeciency, outreach and results. In addition to further development of the Sida supported IR project, the programme now also consits of ILO’s Better Work, Vision Zero Fund and SCORE (productivity improvement training) programmes. The Better Work Programme is a unique partnership between the International Labour Organization (ILO) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). It was launched in August 2006 in order to improve labour standards and competitiveness in global supply chains. The programme assists enterprises improve practices based on core ILO labour standards and national labour law. It does this with a strong emphasis on improving worker-management cooperation, working conditions and social dialogue. Enhanced respect for labour standards helps enterprises meet the social compliance demands of global buyers, improves conditions for workers, and helps firms become more competitive by increasing productivity and quality. The Vision Zero Fund (VZF), an initiative of the Group of Seven (G7) countries, aims at preventing work-related deaths, injuries and diseases in sectors operating in or aspiring to join global supply chains (GSCs). VZF’s main objective is to increase collective public and private action aimed at fostering and enhancing concrete occupational safety and health (OSH) prevention activities in businesses operating in low- and middle-income countries. SCORE (Sustaining Competitive and Responsible Enterprises) is an ILO programme that promotes productivity, competitiveness and decent work in emerging economies. In Ethiopia, SCORE will provide productivity trainings with a focus on improving resource (both human and material) productivity and efficiency of workers and key processes in the production system. The training module will include, among others, Lean and Kaizen principles and practical use in actual factory set-up, flow improvement, productive maintenance, continuous quality improvement, waste elimination to reduce cost and environmental safeguard. The intervention will be implemented in two phases. The proposed Project Document describes the first phase of the project (2019-2023), which will focus on the textile and apparel sector. Building on the lessons learned from the intervention in the garment and textile sector, the programme will also conduct a pre-feasibility assessment of the industrial relations, working conditions and productivity challenges in the newly established agro-industrial parks, which will provide the possibility to expand operations and ensure linkages between agriculture and manufacturing industries. For example, the capacity building packages produced by the programme will be customised to the needs of the agriculture sector, and the programme will facilitate exchanges and learning between the garment and agro-industrial parks. Furthermore, the intervention will maintain close links with ILO’s ongoing work in support of the implementation of Ethiopia’s Jobs Compact, which will expand employment opportunities to refugees, including in identified industrial sectors, such as textile and apparel.

The reporting covers the One-ILO program from both the Vision Zero Fund and the SCORE program. Sweden's funds are non earmarked and largely contribute to shared salary cost, capacity building initiatives, technical assistance to the labour and employment Bureaus and gender initiatives. During the reporting period, the programme continued to face challenges due to political and civil conflict in Ethiopia and AGOA suspension resulting from the conflicts.
Integrated Summary of Evaluation Validated Results
The final evaluation confirms that the ONEILOSIRAYE Programme delivered strong and measurable results across factory, sectoral, and national levels.
At the factory level, evidence shows clear progress in improving workplace compliance, safety, gender equality, and productivity. Seventyone percent of participating factories successfully implemented sound humanresource and occupationalsafety systems, surpassing the 70% target. Unionisation also expanded, with membership rising from 8% to 16%, and access to justice improved significantly as the number of workers receiving legal aid increased from 11 in 2021 to 605 in 2024.
Overall compliance trends were positive: general noncompliance fell from 19% to 9.5%, while genderrelated noncompliance dropped from 6% to 1.3%. Factory managers and workers reported a noticeable strengthening of zerotolerance approaches to harassment and improved workplace cooperation.
At the sectoral level, the programme contributed to stronger socialdialogue mechanisms and enhanced representation across the garment and textile sector. Fiftythree factories established registered trade unions, and 143 lawenforcement personnel were trained to respond more effectively to genderbased violence. More than 600 workers accessed legal support through newly established call centres and grievance mechanisms in major industrial parks, contributing to improved dispute resolution and broader engagement of workers and employers in structured dialogue. These efforts reinforced wellbeing and strengthened the foundations for inclusive sector governance.
At the national level, the programme advanced key labourpolicy reforms and institutional capacity. Major documentssuch as the revised national OSH Directive, the updated Occupational Disease List, and the draft minimumwage mechanismwere finalised and progressed to ministerial review.
Labourinspection systems were significantly strengthened through the training of 150 inspectors, 424 conducted inspections, and the development of a new Labour Inspection Information Management System. The programme also facilitated closer alignment between the Ministry of Labour and Skills and the Ministry of Health by helping identify and resolve legal inconsistencies related to workplace health and safety.
These improvements contributed to broader system strengthening across ministries, universities, regional labour authorities, trade unions, and industrialpark institutions, supporting longterm sustainability and the continued advancement of decent work.
Institutional Strengthening:
Ministry of Labour and Skills (MoLS): Strengthened through the rollout of the Labour Inspection Information Management System (LMIS), updated inspection workflows, and extensive OSH, labour law, and dispute resolution training. The Ministry now leads implementation of the national OSH Directive and Occupational Disease List.
Ministry of Industry (MoI): Integrated womens leadership programming and co-led national daycare standard development. MoI trainers deliver workplace cooperation and gender trainings independently.
Kaizen Excellence Centre (KEC): Fully embedded SCORE into national SME support services, created a quality assurance team, trained 50 staff, and developed a revenue-generating model. A national training facility was established for broader regional use.
Courts, Labour Relations Boards, and Regional Authorities: Built capacity through training on arbitration, conciliation, OSH directives, and the labour proclamation. Regional labour bureaus gained tools for industrial relations and inspection.
CETU (Trade Unions): Gender policy revised, union leaders trained on gender-responsive CBAs, and peer learning established.
Hawassa Industrial Park Investors Association (HIPIA): Strengthened in collective bargaining, service delivery, and market promotion to buyers. Hired staff (data verifier, housing support, orientation officers) to enhance worker retention.
Universities (Bahir Dar, Hawassa): Established legal aid centres, conducted research, and rolled out labour dispute settlement training manuals.
Assessment:
The programme made substantial progress in improving worker wellbeing, particularly in safety, gender equality, and access to rights. Significant advances included the finalisation of national OSH frameworks, strengthened factory OSH systems, expanded legal aid services, and strong outcomes from womens leadership programmes. Gender equality measures were widely adopted, and grievance resolution improved notably. However, gains in worker income and representation were more limited: union density and the number of CBAs remained below targets, and structural constraints on wagessuch as the absence of a minimum wagepersisted despite ongoing policy dialogue. Growth has been described as being inhibited by factory resistance, turnover of union leaders and low capacity of workers.
Industry productivity and competitiveness showed the strongest and most consistent achievements, surpassing nearly all targets. The SCORE productivity programme reached almost double the planned number of SMEs and was fully embedded within national institutions, leading to sustained productivity gains of 2040%, job creation, and improved management systems across the sector. Workplace cooperation training, leadership development, and improved HRM/OSH systems all contributed to a more efficient and competitive industrial environment, demonstrating both immediate enterprise-level impact and longterm institutional sustainability.
Accountability and transparency in labour administration were also significantly strengthened, driven by major institutional reforms and capacity-building initiatives. The rollout of the Labour Inspection Information Management System (LMIS), new inspection workflows, and extensive training for inspectors and labour authorities improved data quality, consistency, and oversight. National OSH directives and tools were finalised, and dispute resolution capacity was enhanced through strengthened labour boards, legal aid centres, and judicial training.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
